docs:
Media contracts for zen codecs: what a video (and later audio) codec, a
container and a pipeline say to each other.

`no_std + alloc`, no I/O, no async, no codec implementations. The image
contract in [`zencodec`] stays as it is; this crate adds the pieces video
needs and reuses the image side's shapes wherever they fit:

- [`packet`]: compressed access units with optional timestamps, container
  random-access evidence and configuration epochs.
- [`track`]: codec identity separate from the container, validated track
  descriptions.
- [`frame`]: decoded frames as owned, refcounted handles over backend
  pictures, with planar views and an immutable per-frame interpretation.
- [`session`]: codec sessions with explicit backpressure (`send` /
  `receive`), drain at end of input, and discard-only reset.
- [`container`]: a sans-I/O [`Demuxer`](container::Demuxer) speaking the
  image decoders' `Input`/`InputRequest` dialogue (so every `zencodec-io`
  driver serves it), and a [`Muxer`](container::Muxer) whose bytes are
  pulled like a streaming image encoder's.
- [`adapt`]: the animation traits as a layer over demuxer + decoder and
  encoder + muxer.

Time comes from [`zencodec::time`]. Design and rationale:
`docs/media-design.md` in the repository; the rules every implementation
follows: `docs/media-contract.md`.

Animation as a layer over the video model, both ways, through the real
zencodec animation traits.

- [`VideoAnimationDecoder`] implements
  [`AnimationFrameDecoder`] over a [`Demuxer`] and a [`VideoDecoder`]. A
  frame lasts until the next one's presentation timestamp; the last one
  lasts the explicit `final_duration` (IVF, WebM and MP4 do not reliably
  record it). Frames carry their timestamp in [`AnimationFrame::pts`].
- [`AnimationVideoEncoder`] implements [`AnimationFrameEncoder`] over a
  [`VideoEncoder`] and a [`Muxer`]. Durations become timestamps on the
  encoder's clock, exactly or not at all
  ([`UnsupportedOperation::AnimationTiming`]). Its
  [`begin`](AnimationFrameEncoder::begin) and `pending_output` map onto
  the muxer's pull output, so animation output streams when the muxer's
  does.

Turning planes into a packed canvas and back is a colour conversion, and
colour conversion belongs to zenpixels-convert, not to a codec contract.
The adapters take it as a [`RenderFrame`] / [`CaptureFrame`]; [`Gray8`]
is the identity for 8-bit monochrome.

A [`Demuxer`] is sans-I/O and speaks the image decoders' dialogue: the
driver offers an [`Input`], the demuxer takes a prefix and either yields a
[`DemuxEvent`] or names what it [`requested`](Demuxer::requested) next.
[`DemuxStage`] makes any demuxer a [`zencodec_io::ByteStepper`], so every
`zencodec-io` cursor (slice, `ReadAt` with coalesced ranges, `Read`,
async) drives it; a container that needs its index first (an MP4 with
`moov` at the end) asks for that range and declares
[`AccessPattern::RandomAccess`].

A [`Muxer`] takes packets and lets the caller pull its bytes through
`pending_output` / `consume_output` / `take_output`, as a streaming image
encoder does. [`Muxer::begin`] says, through [`MuxTiming`], whether bytes
stream and whether `finish` patches earlier bytes (sizes, offsets); a
caller whose destination cannot seek back passes
[`MuxHint::forward_only`] and gets a layout without patches, or a refusal
at `begin`.

Checked synchronous container output for forward writers and seekable files.

[`PreparedOutput::new`] requires exact packet timing and owns the actual begun
muxer and destination without publishing its header. [`PreparedOutput::publish`]
consumes that preparation. [`Output::new`] combines those steps for callers
that do not need a policy decision between them. Unsupported timing is an
error, never a fallback to container-chosen timing.

```
use zencodec_media::{container::Muxer, output::{Failure, Forward, Output, Stats},
    packet::Packet, track::TrackInfo};
fn write<M: Muxer, W: std::io::Write>(
    muxer: M, writer: W, tracks: &[TrackInfo], packets: impl IntoIterator<Item = Packet>,
) -> Result<Stats, Failure> {
    let pulse = &zencodec::how_far::NoPulse;
    let mut output = Output::new(muxer, Forward(writer), tracks, &pulse)?;
    for packet in packets { output.send(packet, &pulse)?; }
    output.finish(&pulse)
}
```

To ask policy before any write, replace `Output::new` with
[`PreparedOutput::new`], retain the result while deciding, then call
[`PreparedOutput::publish`]. Use [`SeekBack::new`] instead of [`Forward`] for
a file whose current position is the start of this output.

These drivers may block on `Write`. Byte availability does not establish safe
encoder backpressure: finish or separately qualify upstream raw-buffer retention
before sending packets to a slow writer. No whole-operation memory bound is
implied. Dropping either state does not implicitly finish or publish.

A [`Packet`] is what a demuxer yields and a decoder takes, and what an
encoder yields and a muxer takes. It is never a picture: a decoder may
produce zero, one or several frames per packet, and may produce them
later (reordering, hidden frames, show-existing).

The payload is a [`PacketPayload`]: an owned `Vec`, or a range of a shared
buffer, so a demuxer can hand out slices of one read without copying and
a backend can take an owned `Vec` without copying either. A consumer that
accepts a packet takes its payload ([`Packet::take`]); one that pushes
back leaves it in place for the retry.

Codec sessions: packets in, frames out ([`VideoDecoder`]); frames in,
packets out ([`VideoEncoder`]).

The protocol, for both directions:

- `send` offers one input. [`SendStatus::Accepted`] means the session
  took it (a packet's payload is taken; a frame handle is cloned).
  [`SendStatus::ReceivePending`] means "receive first": the input is left
  untouched for the retry, and at least one `receive` now returns
  [`Receive::Ready`]. That is the backpressure: a session never queues
  without bound and never blocks.
- `receive` returns one output, [`Receive::NeedInput`], or, after
  `end_input` and once everything is drained, [`Receive::EndOfStream`],
  which is stable.
- `end_input` declares the end; it is idempotent. Sending after it is a
  [`ProtocolViolation::SendAfterEnd`].
- A decoder's `reset` discards queued input, output and references and
  keeps the configuration; frames already returned stay valid. Seeking is
  `reset` and `configure` (to re-inject a sequence header), then packets
  from the new position.

Sessions do no I/O, need no async runtime and know nothing about
containers. Work calls take a `&dyn zencodec::Pulse`; [`FusedDecoder`] makes errors
and cancellation terminal until a successful `reset`. [`FusedEncoder`]
makes encoder errors terminal; a fresh encoder starts a new operation.
